item.title: Slides: longer engagements, 6 to 48 hours
item.description: Issue #42 asked what it would take to run our TMA on engagements of 6 to 48 hours. On four
item.content:encoded:
Issue #42 asked what it would take to run our TMA on engagements of 6 to 48 hours. On four simulated engagements (seed 348), every standing system ran to the end, on windows of the size it was built for. The time-late control keeps its accuracy at every length. Running it on a whole long period does not work as written, and several parts of the code assume one ownship zig. An investigation, not a gate. Spec: specs/023-long-engagements/.

What was built​

  • A long-engagement simulator (src/tma2/long/sim.py), separate from generator 0.6.0, whose output stays byte-identical. The target follows Annex B's statistics. The ownship turns at the start of each 20–40 minute leg and keeps the target at 3–25 km, steering on the true target position.
  • Windows (src/tma2/long/windows.py) in the form every estimator already reads, and C″'s zig veto applied at every ownship turn.
  • Real-time and time-late runners (src/tma2/long/realtime.py, timelate.py), the tma2-long CLI and the long.yml workflow.
  • Long-engagement sections on the viewer and the time-late page, precomputed in Python.
  • Research note 12 (docs/research/12-long-engagements.md) and the record experiments/20261117-long/ (tables.md generated from summary.json).

What was found​

6 h12 h24 h48 h
time-late ctl, median range error2.0%1.9%2.7%1.6%
time-late C″20.5%15.0%8.5%9.0%
real-time E, every 10 min17.4%17.5%14.3%20.9%
real-time C″23.2%17.1%13.2%19.9%
real-time IMM (answered)19.0% (1.00)35.2% (1.00)15.0% (0.96)30.9% (0.81)
  • ctl on one long period: 1 min for half an hour, 114 min for 6 hours, and at most ten manoeuvres (6 hours held 16).
  • The real-time model re-solves its 2-hour window for every estimate: 27–37 s on one core.
  • The IMM over the whole engagement took 426 s at 48 hours against 6 s at 6; the cause is not established.
  • The Cramér–Rao bound over a whole engagement needs 4.5 GB at 48 hours.

What was not achieved​

  • One engagement per duration: these are anecdotes, not rates.
  • The scenario is kind: the ownship steers on the truth, contact is never lost, one target.
  • No whole-engagement solve, and E does not run in the browser on these engagements.

What comes next (the owner's choice)​

Recommended: carry state between windows (each window starts from the previous solution), then an incremental C so a real-time estimate costs the same at hour 48 as at hour 2; realism (an ownship steering on its own solution, contact gaps, a second target) before any registered study. The next fresh seed is 349.

Figures: scripts/research/long_charts.py, with a sidecar beside each SVG.

item.title: Kickoff: longer engagements, 6 to 48 hours
item.description: Issue #42 asks what it takes to apply our TMA to engagements of 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours, and to
item.content:encoded:
Issue #42 asks what it takes to apply our TMA to engagements of 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours, and to show them on the viewer and time-late pages. This task is an investigation: it simulates one engagement of each length, runs the standing systems on them as they are, measures what that costs and how they do, and lists the implementation challenges. Spec: specs/023-long-engagements/.

Where we are​

  • Every engagement so far is 40 to 120 minutes with one ownship zig (MAN2, generator 0.6.0).
  • The real-time model E (Gate 2) is carried and runs in the browser. Its exported graph takes exactly 720 rows: two hours of 10-second bearings.
  • The time-late track closed with the classical control ctl standing, decided on periods of 20 to 120 minutes.

Where this task moves to​

  • Acceptance (no gate, nothing trained, no GPU):
    • four engagements (seed 348, fresh) of 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours, with Annex B's target manoeuvres and an ownship that turns at each 20–40 minute leg and keeps the target in range;
    • every system runs to the end of each: real-time every 10 minutes on a sliding 2-hour window (E, C″, one leg) and over the whole engagement (IMM); time-late ctl on a chain of 2-hour windows, stitched;
    • a research note listing the challenges, each measured where it can be;
    • long-engagement sections on /viewer and /timelate.
  • Plan:
    • a separate simulator, so generator 0.6.0 stays byte-identical (its table holds 32 target changes; 48 hours needs about 100);
    • windows cut from the long engagement in the form every estimator already reads;
    • the runs on CI (about 14 CPU-hours for the real-time part alone);
    • a timing of ctl on single periods of 0.5 to 6 hours, to show why it is run on windows.
  • Risks: ctl may be too slow on long periods to time at all; four engagements are anecdotes, so the note will not claim rates.

How progress will be shown​

The slides post will carry the tracks of the 48-hour engagement, error against time for each system, run time against period length, and the list of challenges.

item.title: Slides: the site, published, with persistent PR previews
item.description: The site is published to GitHub Pages on every merge. A new time-late page shows
item.content:encoded:
The site is published to GitHub Pages on every merge. A new time-late page shows the standing time-late system's tracks. Every pull request now keeps a preview, listed on PR previews. Spec: specs/022-site-publishing/.

What was built​

  • .github/workflows/pages.yml:
    • Merges to main publish the site at the root of gh-pages.
    • Each same-repository PR publishes its own build at pr/<n>/, and the copy is kept after the PR completes.
    • Closing a PR updates its state in pr/index.json.
    • A manual run builds a preview for an earlier PR.
    • Deploys run one at a time.
  • /previews lists every PR with a preview: its state, a link to the preview, and links to the blog posts it added or changed, opened in that preview.
  • /timelate draws whole-period tracks from spec 016's test record (seed 341, used):
    • the 20 first stored periods each of Annex B targets, 2% wild bearings and a shifted manoeuvre prior;
    • the standing control, C″, the true-history fit and the learned model;
    • true and declared manoeuvres on a timeline;
    • per-period errors, checked against the record by a unit test.

What was not achieved​

  • PRs before this one have no preview until the manual backfill is run for them.
  • The page's medians are over every stored row, not the scorer's rows, so they are not the record's figures. The page says so.

item.title: Kickoff: publish the site, a time-late page, persistent PR previews
item.description: The site has been built in CI but never published. This task publishes it to GitHub Pages on
item.content:encoded:
The site has been built in CI but never published. This task publishes it to GitHub Pages on every merge. It adds a time-late page that shows the standing system's whole-period tracks, and gives every pull request a persistent preview, listed in an index. Spec: specs/022-site-publishing/.

Where we are​

  • Specs 020 and 021 put the carried model in the browser. The time-late account closed the time-late track with a classical control standing.
  • None of this is online. gh-pages holds only the first commit's README.

Where this task moves to​

  • Acceptance:
    • after a merge, the root, the blog, /viewer, /timelate and /previews return 200;
    • a PR's preview and its post links work while it is open and after it is merged;
    • the time-late page's errors equal the record's, recomputed.
  • Plan:
    • a pages.yml workflow deploys to gh-pages: the root on main, and pr/<n>/ for each same-repository PR;
    • an index file and a /previews page;
    • the time-late page, from spec 016's test record;
    • a manual backfill for earlier PRs.
  • Risks: the branch grows by a site per PR, though git stores identical files once. Pages must serve the gh-pages branch. It does today, since it serves the README.

How progress will be shown​

The PR for this task is the first with a preview. Its slides post links the published pages.

Updates​

  • 2026-11-16, after the owner's review of the preview:
    • The time-late page shows each system's solution whole, as one fit to all the period's bearings. The time slider is gone; start and end markers and 10-minute ticks remain.
    • The viewer says it is the real-time model and points to the time-late page.
  • 2026-11-17, issue 44: each PR now carries a comment linking its preview at pr/<n>/, the blog posts it adds or changes and the commit it was built from. One comment per PR, found by a hidden marker and edited in place on every push, as the argonautical repository does it. A backfill run publishes without commenting.
  • 2026-11-17, issue 41 (the owner's request):
    • The track plots (the viewer, time-late and the long-engagement sections on both pages) zoom with the mouse wheel about the cursor. A drag pans, a double click resets, and buttons do the same for touch and keyboard users. Markers and line widths keep their size; the scale bar follows the zoom.
    • The viewer can show the measured bearings received so far, one a minute with the latest in bold. They come from the engagement's scenario file, checked against the manifest's digest. The time-late data carry no bearings, so that page has zoom only.
    • Both plots now use one scale on both axes. Before, north–south was drawn at 0.79 (viewer) and 0.73 (time-late) of east–west, which bent courses and squashed the 1-σ ellipse.

item.title: Slides: the carried model end to end in the browser
item.description: The viewer can now run Gate 2's carried model live, from bearings alone. The
item.content:encoded:
The viewer can now run Gate 2's carried model live, from bearings alone. The classical segmenter C, E-s's evidence and E-w's estimate all run in the browser. On 30 check scenarios every decision matches Python's. Spec: specs/021-browser-segmenter/. Record: experiments/20261116-port/.

What was built​

  • A JavaScript port of C's host code from its frozen Python (site/static/viewer-data/js/):
    • the per-row least squares and the GLR statistic;
    • the ownship segmenter O and E-s's features;
    • the search, its Levenberg–Marquardt segment costs and the dynamic programme;
    • nominations, confirmation, intervals and the hand-over.
  • The physics layer at confirmation's settings, exported as its own graph. Its three-runtime conformance passes, with cost agreeing to 7e-15 in the browser.
  • A live mode on the page: a module worker runs the whole pipeline with progress and a cancel, draws the live trail beside the others, and compares it with Python.
  • The checks:
    • a committed dump of every intermediate for 30 scenarios of used seed 319;
    • a Node comparison stage by stage (CI job browser-port);
    • live mode on every demo engagement in Chromium (viewer_leg.mjs).

What the figures show​

  • Agreement: identical segmentations on 1,770 of 1,770 scored rows, for C and for E.

  • Margins: the largest difference in a confirmation cost drop per scenario, against the smallest margin of any decision from its threshold.

    • The differences are 5.4e-9 or less, except one of 1.3e-4.
    • The margins are 0.152 or more.

    The gap explains the identity. It does not guarantee it: an engagement with a decision within 1e-3 of its threshold could differ, and the check would say so.

  • Stages: live mode takes 25 to 93 s an engagement on one WASM thread. Confirmation is most of it. The first row waits for confirmation: about 76 s on the busiest engagement, which misses the spec's one-minute target for the first row.

What was not achieved​

  • Pasting a scenario of one's own (the spec's third story, P3) is not built.

  • Some intermediates differ without changing a decision:

    • one row's least squares on ordinal 22 lands in another minimum;
    • search cost tables differ by up to 22% where fits hit their iteration cap.
    • the GLR statistic differs by up to 2.9. At one row (ordinal 1, row 256) it lies on the other side of the alarm threshold from Python's. No nomination changed there, but one could on another scenario, and the check would fail.

    These are recorded in the research notes, not hidden.

What comes next​

The owner's choice. The remaining options from spec 020's write-up are real data, several periods of one target, and ownship advice.

item.content:encoded:
The owner chose to port the classical segmenter C to JavaScript, so that the viewer runs the carried model from bearings alone, with nothing prepared in Python. Spec: specs/021-browser-segmenter/. Nothing is trained, no gate, no fresh seed.

Where we are​

  • Spec 020's viewer runs E-w's exported graph in the browser, on C's hand-over shipped from Python. CI checks it against Python to 3e-6 on 181 rows.
  • The carried model is still Gate 2's E: E-s's evidence, C's confirmation, and E-w into the physics layer. E-s and E-w are exported graphs. C is Python.

Where this task moves to​

  • SRD §1 (the viewer) and constitution VI (the browser as a runtime).
  • Acceptance:
    • on at least 30 scenarios of seed 319, the browser's segmentation equals Python's on at least 95% of scored rows;
    • every difference is traced to a decision near its threshold;
    • the live estimate matches Python's where the segmentation does;
    • the busiest demo engagement finishes in under 10 minutes on a CI runner.
  • Plan:
    1. Export the physics layer as a cost graph, with three-runtime conformance.
    2. Port C's host code to JavaScript: LS states, GLR, search, confirmation, hand-over.
    3. Write a Python dump of every intermediate and a headless comparison, stage by stage.
    4. Add a live mode on the page, and pasted scenarios if time allows.
    5. Slides.
  • Risks:
    • Speed. C's confirmation needs about 600 physics-layer rows on a busy engagement, about 2.5 minutes in the browser, and E's segmentation as much again.
    • Fragile decisions. A threshold decision can flip on last-bit differences, so the claim is "identical except near the threshold", with the margins reported.
  • Stop condition: if the port cannot reach 95% identical rows for reasons other than near-threshold decisions, the record says so and the page keeps the shipped mode as its default.

How progress will be shown​

  • Each stage's agreement with Python (statistic, costs, decisions) on the check scenarios.
  • The share of identical rows.
  • Every near-threshold decision with its margin.
  • Stage times per engagement.
  • A track plot from live mode beside the shipped one.

item.title: Slides: the carried model, running in a browser
item.description: The last item of the SRD's default plan: a viewer page that runs Gate 2's carried
item.content:encoded:
The last item of the SRD's default plan: a viewer page that runs Gate 2's carried model's exported graph in your browser on six simulated engagements, beside the classical systems. CI checks it row by row against Python. A demonstration, not a result. The figures of record stay in Gate 2's write-up.

What was built​

  • tma2-viewer-data picks six engagements of Gate 2's used test seed 319 by a fixed rule (tma2.viewer.choose):

    • quiet, one manoeuvre, busy;
    • the first where E's median range error over the G5 rows is worse than C″'s;
    • then one more "one manoeuvre" and one more "busy".

    For each engagement, every 60 s from zig + 5 min, it builds:

    • C's segmentation with E-s's evidence, and C's hand-over;
    • from those, the twelve inputs of E-w's exported graph;
    • Python's onnxruntime outputs on them;
    • the truth, and the estimates of one leg, the frozen IMM, C and C″.

    A manifest binds the result by SHA-256. The data are 0.16 MB gzipped, beside a 1.06 MB graph.

  • The page (site/src/pages/viewer.js) runs the graph in ONNX Runtime Web 1.31.1 (WASM, one thread, in a worker). It computes the current time first, then fills in the trail. It checks every file's digest before showing an estimate. The ellipse is off by default and never shown without the Gate 3 warning.

  • CI (onnx-conformance) runs three checks:

    • the page's graph is byte-identical to a fresh export of the carried weights;
    • a fresh Python run reproduces the shipped outputs;
    • the built page in Chromium matches Python on every row (conformance/onnx/viewer_leg.mjs).

What the figures show​

  • Tracks: the busy engagement (ordinal 3) and the one where E loses to C″ (ordinal 6), at the last scored time. The trails are each system's estimate at each scored time, from zig + 5 min.
  • Range error: every system on every engagement. E is close to C and C″ throughout, and is neither best nor worst everywhere. On engagement 5 the one-leg fit is better late on. Six engagements say nothing about which system is better: Gate 2's 4,983 do.
  • Conformance: 181 rows. The browser's state is within 2.7e-6 of Python's, and the covariance on its own scale within 3.2e-6. The flags are identical. Element-wise, one off-diagonal covariance element of one row (engagement 4, row 432, inside an open transition) differs by 3.2e-5, above the constitution's 1e-5. Torch and Python's onnxruntime agree on that row to 7e-8, so the difference is the browser runtime's. Why is not established. The check now gates the covariance relative to its own scale, and reports the element-wise figure on every run (specs/020-browser-viewer/research.md R6).
  • Timing: about 0.27 s a row on one thread. The graph loads in 1 s, the first estimate appears 1.7 s after the page opens, and a whole engagement takes 5 to 15 s. These were measured headless on this project's container; CI's figures go in its step summary.

What was not achieved​

  • C and its confirmation still run in Python. A live viewer would need them ported by hand from the algorithm note.
  • The page shows E's raw covariance, which is overconfident: no calibration was carried (Gates 3 and 4 stopped).
  • The relaxed covariance measure is a change made after the first result. It is stated as such, not hidden.

What comes next​

The SRD's default plan (§7) is complete with this step. What follows is the owner's choice. The records point to:

  • real data;
  • several periods of one target;
  • ownship advice;
  • a port of C for a live viewer.

item.title: Slides: the time-late track as a whole
item.description: The illustrated companion to
item.content:encoded:
The illustrated companion to the account of the time-late track: the standing system, what it gained over the old one, what remains, the attempts to beat it, the last diagnostic, and three periods as tracks, good and bad.

What the figures show​

  • Gains: the old system (C″ read as a track) ÷ the standing control, by kind of target and bearing error, on the test seeds of specs 017 and 018.
  • Remaining: the standing control ÷ a fit told the true manoeuvre history, on three test seeds. A reference, not a bound.
  • Challengers: the standing control ÷ each attempt to beat it, on Annex B and busier targets: the learned model's read-out and its own track (spec 016), the search told the true statistics (017, 018), the prior adapted to the period, declared and hedged (018).
  • Ladder: development work on 130 used periods: the standing control ÷ the search under the broadened prior taking on the true statistics a part at a time, and each part alone; orange ticks are the same ratio without its ten best periods.
  • Three periods as tracks, chosen by a rule in the script: of the 20 stored shifted periods of spec 017's test, those where the standing control is best, median and worst against the old system.

Reproducing the figures​

uv run python scripts/research/tl_synthesis.py --out experiments/20261115-tl-synthesis/tables.md --fig-dir site/static/img/2026-11-15-time-late-synthesis-slides

The script reads only committed records (experiments/20261114-tl4/, 20261114-tl5/, 20261115-tl6/, 20261115-tl7-dev/); each figure's .json sidecar names the inputs' digests and the commit. The data are test seeds 341, 344 and 347, 5-second bearings, generated in their CI runs.

item.title: The time-late track as a whole: what six studies established, and what they did not
item.description: Between 11 and 15 November the project ran six studies on the time-late consumer: the
item.content:encoded:
Between 11 and 15 November the project ran six studies on the time-late consumer: the analyst who wants the target's whole track over a period after the fact, not the best estimate now. Each has its own write-up and its own panel review. This is the account of all six together: what is standing, what was shown, what was withdrawn, and what was never tested. Figures are from the committed test records and their panel reviews; the table of record is generated by a script. The illustrated companion is the slides post.

The question​

Given every bearing of a period of 20 to 120 minutes, at 5-second intervals, say where the target was, its course and its speed at every moment, and when it manoeuvred. Nothing was trained except in one study, which says so. Every result is on simulated data from one generator.

What is standing​

The classical control (study L's ctl, declared):

  1. wild bearings are edited out;
  2. the bearing sd is enlarged when the bearings' second differences show the errors are correlated in time;
  3. a search over manoeuvre histories, each fitted with an arc model (a turn at a constant rate, a speed change at a constant rate) and scored by its evidence under Annex B's manoeuvre statistics and under a broadened set, pooled;
  4. a manoeuvre is declared only when it is worth an evidence margin, with a stated 1% chance that the target never manoeuvres.

It replaced "C″ read as a track": the causal segmenter's answer at the end of the period, read backwards.

Its known faults, which a reader should have before trusting it:

  • it calls a one-manoeuvre target quiet more often than the search it grew from: 0.29 against 0.05 with correlated errors, 0.17 against 0.04 with 5% wild bearings;
  • on busier targets it misses about half the manoeuvres;
  • it does nothing under a slowly varying bias;
  • its editing and its enlarged sd know the simulator's error family (wild bearings at 10 sd are edited at 4), and its correlation estimate fires in 8% of clean periods;
  • the evidence it ranks by has an unrepaired fault at the edges of the prior's support;
  • the prior it uses is the simulator's own for Annex B targets.

What was shown​

All ratios are paired per period, in period median range error, on fresh test seeds, unless a line says otherwise.

The search with the arc model and Annex B's statistics roughly halves the old system's error. C″ ÷ search is 1.7 and 2.1 on Annex B targets in the gate and its follow-on (specs 013 and 014), and 2.05 and 2.24 for the repaired search on two later seeds; on busier targets 1.5 to 1.65; 3.1 with 2% of bearings wild. The panels narrowed what that means. It is mostly smoothing with the right motion model and prior, not finding the right history: the search wins where its history is wrong too, it is worse than C″ in about 30% of periods, and refitting C″'s own manoeuvres with the arc model and prior obtains between a third and a half of the gain (specs 014 and 015). A search under a flat prior obtains about four fifths of it: Annex B's statistics themselves are worth about a fifth.

Editing and an honest bearing sd remove most of the damage from bad bearings. Search ÷ control: 1.68 with 2% wild bearings, 2.44 with 5%, 1.33 with correlated errors, 1.70 on targets that hold course (false manoeuvres in 8% of periods against 49%). The outlier and correlated-error gains replicate over a tuning, a validation and a test seed. On clean Annex B targets the control is level with the search or slightly ahead (0.96 on validation; 1.05 [0.99, 1.12] and 1.09 [1.02, 1.18] on two test seeds; the median period is level), and under a slowly varying bias it does nothing (1.00).

Against the old system the standing control is 2.1 to 2.4 times better on Annex B targets, 1.6 to 1.7 on busier targets, about 5 with wild bearings, 2.9 with correlated errors, and level on targets that hold course (seeds 344 and 347).

What remains, against a fit told the true manoeuvre history, depends on how that fit is made. The undeclared control against a reference whose times are free unless it drifts: 1.3 on Annex B targets, 1.2 on targets with larger, rarer manoeuvres, 1.8 to 2.1 on busier targets (three seeds). The declared control against a reference with its times held: 1.6, 1.5 and 2.3 to 2.7 (two seeds). These references are told true times and are not bounds: the control beats them in a quarter of periods on busier targets and in up to nearly a half elsewhere.

On busier targets part of the remainder cannot be closed, and how much depends on where the line is drawn. Over a third of their manoeuvres add less than 20 to the fit's χ² when left out singly (16% on Annex B targets); that single-omission measure is not additive and overstates what is hidden. A reference told only the manoeuvres above the line leaves the control 0.65, 0.44 or 0.14 of its gap to close at lines of 10, 20 and 40; more in course and speed than in range. The closable part sits in the under-a-third of periods where the control misses a manoeuvre the bearings show (spec 017).

Beyond range. The first candidate history is the true one in about 0.64 of Annex B periods. The candidates' stated probabilities are honest on average on Annex B targets and carry only a rank on busier ones. In course and speed the control's gain over the old system is of the same size as in range; for the challengers below, course and speed are given where they differ.

What was tried against the control​

ChallengerAnnex B targetsBusier targetsStudy
Learned whole-period model, its declared read-out (three seeds, 12.5 million periods each)0.81 to 0.820.80 to 0.82016
The same model's own track0.711.01 in range; 0.79 course, 0.77 speed016
Search told the targets' true statistics0.96, 0.981.17, 1.10; 1.15 [1.07, 1.23] pooled over a tuning and two test seeds017, 018
A prior chosen from 30 by the period's evidence0.93; 0.91 [0.84, 0.98] pooled over three seeds1.00 [0.92, 1.08]018
Hedged mean of candidate tracks0.921.00 in range, about 0.9 in course018

Control ÷ challenger; above 1 the challenger is better.

  • The learned model's declared read-out lost in the conditions it was trained on, and won only on targets that hold course (1.06). The panel showed the registered comparison measured its untuned manoeuvre detector: the median period is a tie, and the loss sits where the model declares fewer manoeuvres. Its own track leans on what targets do in general, winning where the bearings say little and losing by three where they say much. "This model with this read-out stops"; a learned proposer inside the search was not tested.
  • The right prior is worth about a tenth to a sixth on busier targets, and not in the typical period. On seed 347 it is better than the control in 53% of periods, over twice as good in 20% and over twice as bad in 13%: two heavy tails that nearly cancel. (Spec 018's record says ten periods of 355 carry 87% of the gain. That statistic drops only the best periods and reads any widely spread ratio as a tail; trimmed at both ends the ratio is unchanged at 1.10.)
  • This evidence, on one period, does not choose among these 30 priors. It does not rank them by accuracy; choosing by groups of periods does no better. The family's cost on Annex B targets is the design's: it lacked Annex B's own prior, which the control has, and its grid was set knowing the test targets' statistics. That a prior cannot be adapted from one period in general was not shown.
  • A hedged mean is not better than a declared history, and its spread could not be stated by one factor.

The last diagnostic​

Spec 018's panel left one thing confounded: the family of priors only refitted a shared set of candidate histories, and it lacked parts of the true statistics. One run on 130 periods already used (seed 347; development work, not a result; nothing in it is separated from 1 in range) looks at both.

  • Refitting was not the handicap. The family member nearest the truth, given a search of its own, is 1.03 [0.91, 1.19] of the control; refitting shared candidates on the same periods it was 1.03 [0.91, 1.19].
  • The gain builds along the ladder, legs first. Taking on the truth's legs, turn sizes, turn rates, speed changes and kinds of manoeuvre in that order gives 0.98, 1.05, 1.06, 1.12, 1.10 and 1.11 [0.94, 1.32]. The first three parts reach the whole prior's figure in range. The other four parts each alone on the broadened prior, without the legs, do nothing (0.92 to 1.00). One order only; a direction, not a decomposition.
  • Neither typical nor a tail. The true prior is better than the control in 55% of these periods, over twice as good in a quarter and over twice as bad in an eighth; trimmed of its ten best and ten worst periods the ratio is 1.14.
  • What the right prior changes steadily is the count: manoeuvres missed fall from 0.52 to 0.36 down the ladder, with false ones near a half a period throughout. In course and speed it is further ahead (1.21 and 1.24, not quite separated).

So the family was not held back by how it was scored. It was short of the truth mainly in how often these targets manoeuvre and how they turn, which it varied, and it still could not be chosen by one period's evidence.

What was withdrawn or corrected along the way​

The record matters as much as the results. In six studies:

  • Spec 013's first reading of the manoeuvre prior was withdrawn: the evidence had been evaluated at a bearings-only fit, which produced thousands of units of artefact. The owner's decision made on that reading went back to the owner.
  • Gate T stopped at validation the first time: its true-history reference started at the truth and stayed there, scoring better than the bound. It was re-registered with a reference fitted from neutral starts.
  • The evidence was wrong five times: evaluated at a bearings-only fit; three small errors in the prior's density; a manoeuvre duration's volume (repaired in spec 015); and the edges of the prior's support (recorded, unrepaired, and applying to every system since). Separately, the rule for manoeuvres cut by a period's edge was wrong in the classing of histories and was repaired in spec 015.
  • Forecasts that were wrong: the share of the search's gain that refitting obtains (0.75 forecast and 0.43 measured in spec 014; 0.50 forecast and 0.33 measured in spec 015); spec 017's forecast that the control would not be separated from the detectable-only reference (it was, though the test value lay inside the tuning interval); spec 018's forecast of a trade. Forecasts read off one tuning run were guesses each time.
  • Rules that measured the wrong thing: spec 016's comparison (a detector, not a model); spec 017's second condition (counts, not cost); spec 018's spread band (its edge sat on the tuning value).
  • Statistics that misled: ratios of medians read as typical gains (spec 013); a gain "carried by its ten best periods" (spec 018 and this spec's first draft), which is what any widely spread ratio looks like when only its best cases are dropped.
  • Words the panels took back: "ceiling", "bound", "upper limit" and "lower limit" for fits told the truth; "ambiguous" for a property of the Laplace evidence; "harm" for a tail with a level median.

What was never tested, and what was tested and left unremedied​

Never tested:

  • a learned proposer inside the search, training through the arc model, a larger training budget, or the control and the learned model's own track combined;
  • a longer history of the same target than one period, to learn its habits;
  • advice to ownship: where the bearings do not show a manoeuvre, ownship's own motion is what would;
  • a family of priors that includes Annex B's own; a working diagnostic that the prior is wrong;
  • the owner's bearing-rate thinning idea (the adaptive rule built for it broke its bins on noise, so the idea itself is untested);
  • a whitened fit or a Huber cost in place of editing and an enlarged sd; a smoothed IMM as a reference; a spread for course and speed; real data of any kind.

Tested and left unremedied: a slowly varying bias (the control does nothing); the evidence's fault at the edges of the prior's support. Thinly tested: whole engagements, on only 60 periods in each of three studies, and the control itself on 60.

What it adds to the project's question​

The project asks whether a learned component can match the classical solution where the simple motion model holds and beat it where it does not. On the time-late consumer the answer is "not shown, at a small budget, with one direct model and one untuned read-out"; as a proposer inside the search a learned model is untested. The large gains came from the motion model (how a manoeuvre unfolds) and from handling bad bearings; the manoeuvre statistics added about a fifth. What is left on targets unlike Annex B's is partly manoeuvres the bearings do not show, and the closable part resisted one learned model and two classical attempts.

A learned approach would be worth trying again if one of three things changed: the data (real bearings, whose errors and target habits no simulator prior states exactly); the information (several periods of the same target, or ownship manoeuvres chosen to reveal it); or the role (a proposer whose suggestions the evidence still judges). None is in the SRD's present scope without the owner's decision.

Records​

Specs 013 to 018: experiments/20261112-gt2/, 20261112-tl2/, 20261113-tl3/, 20261114-tl4/, 20261114-tl5/, 20261115-tl6/, each with review.md. The table of record: experiments/20261115-tl-synthesis/tables.md, generated by scripts/research/tl_synthesis.py. The diagnostic: experiments/20261115-tl7-dev/. Write-ups: Gate T, classical follow-on, repair, controls and a learned model, the shifted-prior gap, a prior that adapts.

Where we are​

  • The last estimator gate is Gate 2, decided by the panel. E beats C by a small margin, and the classical C″ (zig veto and fixed fade) takes most of that. Gates 3 and 4 stopped at validation, so no calibration is carried. E's raw covariance is overconfident: 95% coverage is 0.60.

  • The time-late track ended with a synthesis. Its classical control stands, and it is not an exported artefact.

Where this task moves to​

  • SRD §1 ("a browser viewer on that artefact") and §7 step 5; constitution VI (browser demos run the exported graph in ONNX Runtime Web).
  • Acceptance:
    • every browser output on every demo row agrees with Python's ONNX runtime to 1e-5, checked in CI;
    • the page shows the digests of what it runs;
    • the covariance ellipse is off by default and never shown without the Gate 3 warning;
    • the data stay under 15 MB.

    1. Choose six engagements from Gate 2's used test seed by a fixed rule: quiet, one manoeuvre, busy, and one where E loses to C″.
    2. Write a Python command that builds, for every 60 s from the zig, E-w's inputs from C's hand-over, Python's outputs, and the comparison estimates (batch least squares, IMM, C, C″), with a manifest of digests.
    3. Build a site page that loads the graph in the browser runtime and draws the track plot with a time control.
    4. Add a headless conformance job in CI.

If a whole engagement takes over a minute, the page computes the current time first and fills the trail in behind. The stop condition is a mismatch over 1e-5 that cannot be traced to stale data: that would be a conformance failure of the carried model itself, and is reported as such.

  • Track plots of two demo engagements (the busy one, and the one where E loses to C″), with E's trail beside batch least squares, the IMM and C″, made by tma2-plot from the shipped data.

The owner has chosen option B after spec 018: write up the time-late track (specs 013 to 018) as a whole, with the classical control standing, after one diagnostic on periods already used. Spec: specs/019-time-late-synthesis/. Nothing is trained, no GPU is used and no new seed is generated.

Where we are​

Spec 018 was decided by its panel in one round. A control that chooses among 30 manoeuvre priors by one period's evidence gains nothing on busier targets; the standing control stays. The search told the targets' own statistics is about 1.15 better over three seeds, in a minority of periods. One thing was left confounded: the family's members refitted shared candidates while the true prior had its own search, and the family differed from the truth in parts never varied.

Where this task moves to​

SRD §1 and §5; a line in §9 records the decision (proposed; the owner merges).

  1. A ladder of priors. From the broadened prior to the true one, taking on the busier targets' own statistics a part at a time (legs, turn sizes, turn rates, speed changes, kinds of manoeuvre), each with a search of its own; and each part alone. On 150 shifted periods of seed 347, already used: development work, not a result.
  2. Search against refit. The family member nearest the truth, given its own search, against spec 018's refit of the same periods.
  3. The account. One post covering specs 013 to 018: the standing system, each result as its panel left it, what was withdrawn, the forecasts that were wrong, what was never tested, and what the work adds to the project's founding question.
  4. Independent reviewers check the account against the records; slides; PR.

The time-late track ends here unless the diagnostic shows something the owner wants pursued.

Risks: the parts of a prior may interact, so that no rung "carries" the gain (both the ladder and the single parts are run for that reason); 150 used periods separate only large effects; a synthesis invites tidy conclusions the panels did not allow.

How progress will be shown​

  • The ladder: each rung against the standing control, with the share of its gain in the ten best periods.
  • Search of its own against refit for the nearest member.
  • The track's gains in one chart: old system, search, control, by kind of target and bearing error, from the committed test records of specs 013 to 018.
  • Track plots of example periods chosen by a rule, good and bad.
  • All from committed experiment folders by scripts named in the slides post.

Update, 2026-11-15 (evening). Done. The diagnostic ran on 130 used periods: a search of its own did no better than a refit, and the true prior's gain builds along the ladder, legs first, with nothing separated. Three reviewers checked the account against the records and corrected it. The account and the slides.

item.title: A manoeuvre prior that adapts to the period: no gain, and why one period cannot choose its prior
item.description: Spec 017 said the closable part of the gap on busier targets was largely the prior's. The
item.content:encoded:
Spec 017 said the closable part of the gap on busier targets was largely the prior's. The owner chose to try the classical remedy: a control that infers how the target manoeuvres from the period itself, with a hedged track beside it. It is done, on a fresh seed, with nothing trained. The adaptive control gains nothing on busier targets, so by the rule registered beforehand the standing control stays. My forecast, written from the tuning seed, said otherwise and was wrong. The illustrated companion is the slides post.

What was built​

Two designs, both on the tuning seed. The first ran a search under each of three manoeuvre rates and let the period's evidence choose. It gained nothing: one period did not identify the rate. The second, which was registered, uses a family of 30 priors (how long the legs are, how regular, how large the turns), scores one shared set of candidate histories under each, and declares under the member with the most evidence. Beside it, a hedged track: the weighted mean of every member's candidates, with a stated spread in range.

The plan, code and conditions were bound by digest before the validation and test seeds existed. The conditions read paired period error and coverage, not counts: a lesson from the last panel.

The registered outcome (test seed 347, 1,250 periods)​

Standing control ÷ system, in range (above 1: the system is better):

Split (scored periods)Adaptive, declaredAdaptive, hedged
Shifted (355)1.00 [0.92, 1.08]1.00 [0.93, 1.08]
Shifted 2 (137)1.01 [0.92, 1.11]0.99 [0.89, 1.09]
Annex B (273)0.93 [0.85, 1.01]0.92 [0.84, 1.01]
Held course (172)1.05 [0.98, 1.13]1.02 [0.94, 1.12]
Outliers (93)0.95 [0.79, 1.16]0.94 [0.79, 1.11]
Correlated (93)0.85 [0.71, 1.00]0.89 [0.74, 1.06]

No gain on either busier-target split for either output. The hedged track reads as harm in course on two splits. Its stated spread covers 0.94 of rows on Annex B targets and 0.90 on shifted, at the edge of the registered band. The standing control stays.

On the tuning seed the same comparison was 1.10 and 1.16 on shifted targets. I forecast a trade from that. The 60-period validation seed had already shown 0.95 and 1.04.

What the panel made of it​

Five reviewers recomputed all 36 cells and the registration; all approved with findings. The outcome stands. Several of my secondary sentences did not.

What the null means. The evidence of one period does not rank these priors by how accurate they are. Its preference among the 30 members is nearly flat (the favourite has a probability of about 0.13), and on shifted targets a member's probability and its error are uncorrelated. The member chosen is 1.9 times worse than the member that would have been best in hindsight, and only 3 to 5% better than one sensible fixed member. The choice avoids bad priors. It does not adapt. A period holds two to five manoeuvres: too few to say what kind of target made them.

How tight the null is. The test could have detected a gain of 12%. Pooled over three seeds the declared control is 1.01 [0.95, 1.08]: gains above about 8% are excluded, small ones are not. I wrote that the tuning seed had flattered the design "by all of the effect"; that overstates what one test shows.

The cost on Annex B targets is real and is the design's. Pooled over three seeds: 0.91 [0.84, 0.98]. The standing control searches under Annex B's own prior; my family did not include it. Where the control's answer came from that prior the adaptive control is 0.89; elsewhere 1.05.

The family was not blind. I set its grid after the first tuning run had told me what the first grid lacked, and it sits close to the test splits' own statistics. That favoured it. It gained nothing all the same.

The reference it was chasing is a tail. The search told the true statistics is 1.10 here, 1.15 [1.07, 1.23] over three seeds. Ten shifted periods of 355 carry 87% of that gain, and in 13% of periods it is over twice as bad as the control. I had called it a ceiling. It is not one.

The hedge is not worth having as built. It costs about 10% in course on every split, as a tail, and is level in range. Its spread cannot be stated by one factor: the factor that gave 95% coverage on the tuning seed was 1.95 and on the test seed would be 2.68, both set by about twenty periods. The spread is honest where the candidates disagree and too narrow where the mixture is confident and wrong.

What was wrong in the first record​

  • "The true statistics are worth less than spec 017 found": sampling. Three seeds agree.
  • "The inferred rate barely moves": it moves, by about half the true difference, widely scattered per period.
  • "It loses where the bearings say most": one seed's subgroup, a tail, not repeated.
  • "None of the three is it": the members refit shared candidates and other parts of the prior were never varied.
  • "Not honest by three parts in a thousand": shifted coverage is 0.897 [0.870, 0.923].

What was not delivered​

A family member with Annex B's own prior; a search under each member; unit tests of the runner and the spread code; the tuned IMM and EKF on these periods; a spread for course and speed; a per-period rule for choosing between declared and hedged output that does anything.

What this does and does not show​

It shows that this evidence, on one period, cannot tell which of a family of manoeuvre priors is the right one, and that a hedged mean of candidates is no better than the declared history. On quiet targets the adaptive control invents fewer manoeuvres (3% of periods against 8%), a gain not separated in error and reversed on the tuning seed.

It does not show that priors cannot be adapted: a longer history of the same target, a different evidence, or a family that contained the truth's other dimensions were not tested. It does not show a learned model would fail, though a model facing the same two to five manoeuvres has the same information.

Across specs 013 to 018 the time-late picture is steady. The arc model and Annex B's statistics brought a factor of two over the old system. Editing and an honest bearing sd removed most of the damage from bad bearings. On targets unlike Annex B's, about two thirds of the remaining gap is manoeuvres the bearings do not show, and the rest has now resisted a learned model and a classical one.

What comes next​

The panel's recommendation, which I adopt as mine: stop trying to identify the prior, and write up the time-late track (specs 013 to 018) as a whole, with the classical control standing. The alternatives are in the question put to the owner. A learned proposer or any GPU run would be over-reach.

Records​

experiments/20261114-tl6-tuning/, experiments/20261115-tl6-tuning2/, -tl6-decision/, -tl6-val/ and the test record experiments/20261115-tl6/ (review.md). Seeds 345 to 347 are used; the next fresh seed is 348. Nothing was trained and nothing spent.

item.description: The owner has chosen option B after spec 017: a classical control whose manoeuvre prior is
item.content:encoded:
The owner has chosen option B after spec 017: a classical control whose manoeuvre prior is inferred from the period itself, and beside it a hedged track for the periods where the bearings cannot decide. Spec: specs/018-adaptive-prior/. Nothing is trained and no GPU is used.

Where we are​

Spec 017 was decided by its panel in one round. On targets busier than Annex B says, the standing control is 2.3 times a fit told the true history, and that gap is two things. In about two thirds of periods the limit is manoeuvres the bearings barely show. In under a third the control misses manoeuvres the bearings do show; about half of those are found by the same search when it is told the targets' own statistics (1.17 better overall, at the price of more false manoeuvres). The control stands as the time-late system. Open: a system that is not told the statistics.

Where this task moves to​

SRD §1 and §5; a line in §9 records the owner's decision (proposed; the owner merges).

  1. An adaptive prior. The search runs under several manoeuvre rates and the period's own evidence weighs them, so a busy target is recognised as busy. Not told the split.
  2. Its price. Annex B targets, targets that never manoeuvre, outliers and correlated errors: range, course and speed error, false manoeuvres, one-manoeuvre targets called quiet.
  3. A hedged track. The probability-weighted mean of the candidate histories, across rates too, with a stated spread, and a check that the spread covers the truth as often as it says.
  4. Registration before the fresh seeds (346 validation, 347 test): conditions that can come out either way at the planned size and that read cost, not counts.
  5. Panel, write-up, slides.

If the adaptive control gains on busier targets without harm elsewhere, it is proposed as the standing system. If it gains with harm, the owner decides. If it does not gain, the standing control stays. The hedged track becomes an output only if its spread is honest.

Risks: the inferred rate may follow noise, outliers or correlated errors and invent manoeuvres on quiet targets; the gain available is small (the ceiling is about 1.17 and sits in a minority of periods), so the test may not separate it; a mean of mirror-image candidates is a track no target followed.

How progress will be shown​

  • The inferred rate against the true rate, by split (tuning seed 345, then test 347).
  • Adaptive control ÷ standing control and ÷ the true-prior search on every split, pooled and by kind of period, with period counts.
  • Manoeuvres missed and false for each, at three matching tolerances.
  • The hedged track's error beside the declared track's, and the coverage of its spread.
  • Track plots of periods chosen by a rule in the script.
  • All from committed experiment folders by a script named in the slides post.

Update, 2026-11-15. Done. The first design gained nothing on the tuning seed; a second was registered. Validation on seed 346 passed soundness; the test on seed 347 was scored once and decided by the panel in one round: no gain, the standing control stays. The result and what the panel made of it are in the write-up and the slides.

item.title: Kickoff: the standing time-late control, and is the shifted-prior gap identifiability?
item.description: The owner has chosen the panel's recommendation after study L: the classical control
item.content:encoded:
The owner has chosen the panel's recommendation after study L: the classical control becomes the standing time-late system, and one cheap classical study asks whether the gap left under a shifted manoeuvre prior can be closed by anyone. Spec: specs/017-shifted-gap/. Nothing is trained and no GPU is used.

Where we are​

Study L was decided by its panel in one round. The classical control stands: it removes most of the damage from outliers and correlated bearing errors and from quiet targets. The learned model's reported track beat it nowhere, and the panel showed that loss was the model's untuned manoeuvre detector. Open for every system: on targets that manoeuvre more often and less sharply than Annex B says, the control's error is 1.7 to 2.1 times that of a fit told the true history, with half the manoeuvres missed.

Where this task moves to​

SRD §1 and §5; a line in §9 records the standing system (proposed; the owner merges).

  1. Detectability. For every true manoeuvre, how much worse the bearings are fitted when it is left out of the true history. No search, no evidence approximation.
  2. The gap, split. A reference told only the detectable manoeuvres. The part of the gap that remains for it is identifiability; the part between it and the control is what a better search or evidence could win.
  3. The true prior. The control's search given the shifted targets' own statistics: what knowing them is worth.
  4. Registration of the rule, thresholds and sizes before the fresh seeds (343 validation, 344 test), with the rule's power stated.
  5. What study L's record owes: the scored weights' digests, the export check on the trained models, IMM and EKF tracks beside, a reference fitted to edited bearings, tests for the runner and scorer.
  6. Panel, write-up, slides.

If the gap is mostly identifiability, the learned-proposer idea is not taken and the time-late track is written up. If it is mostly attainable, a proposer study using the three trained models is proposed to the owner.

Risks: "detectable" depends on a threshold (three are registered and the result is given at each); the reference told the true history drifts in a quarter of shifted periods (its times are held, and the share stated); a split may come out mixed, which is a result.

How progress will be shown​

  • The distribution of detectability for Annex B and shifted manoeuvres, and the control's miss rate against it (tuning 342, then test 344).
  • The gap as two stacked parts per split and threshold, with intervals.
  • The true-prior search beside the control.
  • Track plots of periods with undetectable manoeuvres, chosen by a rule in the script.
  • All from committed experiment folders by a script named in the slides post.

Update, 2026-11-14 (evening). Done. Validation on seed 343 passed soundness; the test on seed 344 was scored once and decided by the panel in one round. The result and what the panel made of it are in the write-up and the slides.

item.title: Why the time-late control is twice the reference on busier targets: part hidden manoeuvres, part the wrong prior
item.description: Study L left one gap open on both sides: on targets that manoeuvre more often and less
item.content:encoded:
Study L left one gap open on both sides: on targets that manoeuvre more often and less sharply than Annex B says, the classical control is about twice a fit told the true history. The owner asked for one cheap classical study of whether that gap is identifiability, before anyone considers a learned proposer. It is done, on a fresh seed, with nothing trained. The answer is not one number. In about two thirds of periods the limit is manoeuvres the bearings barely show; in under a third the control misses manoeuvres the bearings do show, and at least half of those misses are the prior's, not the search's. The illustrated companion is the slides post.

What was measured​

For every true manoeuvre, its detectability: how much the χ² of the true history's fit rises when that one manoeuvre is left out, the others' times held. Bearings only, no prior, no search. Then three kinds of reference:

  • a fit told every manoeuvre (ref-full);
  • fits told only the manoeuvres above a detectability of 10, 20 or 40;
  • the control's own search given the busier targets' true statistics.

The thresholds bracket what the evidence charges for a manoeuvre under Annex B's prior (about 22). The plan, code and estimands were bound by digest before the validation and test seeds existed. No decision rule was registered, because on tuning data the plan's rule was a coin's toss; instead the logic of the recommendation was fixed in advance.

The numbers (test seed 344; shifted split, 451 scored periods)​

Threshold 10Threshold 20Threshold 40
Share of true manoeuvres under it0.280.370.47
Not being told them costs1.341.582.02
Control ÷ the reference not told them1.70 [1.52, 1.90]1.43 [1.28, 1.61]1.12 [0.99, 1.27]
Attainable share of the control's gap0.650.44 [0.33, 0.54]0.14

The whole gap is 2.27 [2.04, 2.55]. On Annex B data 0.16 of manoeuvres are under 20; on these targets 0.37 are. The control misses 0.83 of those and 0.18 of the ones above 40. Given the targets' own statistics, the same search is 1.17 [1.06, 1.29] better than the control.

By the logic fixed beforehand, a proposer study would be recommended only if the control were separated from the threshold-20 reference by more than 1.10 and it missed over a third of the manoeuvres above 40. The first held (against my forecast); the second did not (0.18). Output of the logic: not recommended.

What the panel made of it​

Five reviewers recomputed everything; all approved with findings. The registration held and every number reproduces. They changed the reading in four ways.

The pooled split is two kinds of period. Where some manoeuvre is under 20 (336 periods), the control is only 1.16 times the reference that is not told it: there the limit is what the bearings can show. Where nothing is under 20 (115 periods), the control is 2.65 times the reference. Cut the other way: in the 134 periods where the control misses a manoeuvre above 20 it is 2.73 times the reference, and those periods carry 83% of the attainable gap; in the other 317 it is 1.09. "0.44 attainable" is an average of "mostly identifiability" and "all attainable". By geometry, the attainable share is 0.70 where the bound is tight and 0.20 where it is loose.

My rule's second condition measured the wrong thing. It counted manoeuvres; the cost is per period. And it depends on how closely a found manoeuvre must match in time: the miss rate above 40 is 0.30 at 60 seconds, 0.18 at the registered 120, 0.11 at 240. The "no" is the rule's output. It does not follow from the evidence, and at a tuning value of 0.18 the condition could hardly have fired. I registered it; that was a poor choice.

The attainable part is at least half a prior problem. Of the 138 detectable manoeuvres the control misses, the same search under the right prior finds 66. Where it finds more, it is 2.6 times better; elsewhere, 1.07. In most periods with such a miss the control declares fewer manoeuvres than happened: it under-counts because Annex B's prior tells it these targets are quiet. A learned proposer feeding the same evidence would mostly be vetoed by it.

The measure is not a bound in either direction. Detectability is not additive: on 39 periods a reviewer refitted, leaving out two or three "undetectable" manoeuvres together cost 20 or more in 44% (in one case 18, 0.2 and 2 singly, 2,481 together). So the "hidden" share and the cost of hiding are overstated. And the references are flattered by being told true times: with the right history the control is still 1.6 to 1.7 times the full reference. I wrote that one estimand was an upper limit and another a lower limit; neither is.

What was wrong in the first record​

  • "The tuning seed differed by more than its intervals": false. The test's values lie inside the tuning intervals. A point estimate from 134 periods was read as a forecast.
  • The IMM and EKF ratios (4.8 to 22) were on the 40% of periods where a filter has a state on most rows; on common rows they are 3.8 to 10.5. Far behind either way.
  • Shifted 2's "mostly attainable" rests on one clipped reference and 19 manoeuvres.

What was not delivered​

The split under each way of fitting the reference; course and speed in the estimands (the panel's recomputation: more attainable than range); a joint detectability; unit tests for the new runner and the detectability code; a smoothed IMM.

What this does and does not show​

It shows that on busier targets a good part of the gap cannot be closed by any detector working from these bearings, that the closable part is concentrated in a minority of periods, and that the cheapest lever on it is the manoeuvre prior, not the search.

It does not give "the share that is identifiability": that number moves from 0.35 to 0.86 with the threshold, and the measure behind it is biased both ways. It does not show a proposer would fail, only that the evidence would veto much of what it proposed. And the 1.17 for the right prior is one seed, a minority of periods, and bought with more false manoeuvres (0.48 a period against 0.34).

What comes next​

The panel's recommendation, which I adopt as mine: a prior that adapts to the period (a manoeuvre rate estimated from the period itself, or a mixture over rates), classical, on CPU, registered against the standing control with the true-prior search as its ceiling and the false-manoeuvre rate on quiet targets reported. Beside it, a hedged track for the periods where the limit is identifiability. A GPU proposer now would be over-reach. The choice is the owner's.

Records​

experiments/20261114-tl5-tuning/, -tl5-decision/, -tl5-val/ and the test record experiments/20261114-tl5/ (review.md). Seeds 342 to 344 are used; the next fresh seed is 345. Nothing was trained and nothing spent.

item.title: Time-late, classical controls and a learned model: the controls stand, and what the learned model's loss is made of

item.content:encoded:
The owner asked for two things at once: the classical controls the last panel wanted, and a learned whole-period model trained in parallel under a plan fixed before any result. Both are done. On a fresh test seed the learned model's reported track beats the classical control on no split and loses to it on clean data, so by the registered rule the classical controls stand and the learned track stops. The review panel approved that outcome and changed what it means: the loss is not a typical period, it is the model's untuned manoeuvre detector, and the comparison we registered was narrower than "learned against classical". The illustrated companion is the slides post.

What was built​

Classical controls, nothing trained, composed from the search spec 015 left standing:

  • wild bearings edited out before the search;
  • one larger bearing sd when the bearings' second differences show the errors are correlated in time;
  • the search run under Annex B's manoeuvre prior and a broadened one, pooled;
  • a manoeuvre declared only when it is worth an evidence margin of 1, with a stated 1% chance that the target never manoeuvres;
  • a hedged track: the probability-weighted mean of the candidates.

Settings came from a tuning seed. The combined control is not told which condition it is in.

A learned model: a bidirectional transformer reading a whole period of 5-second bearings and giving the target's state every 30 seconds and a manoeuvre probability. Three seeds, 12.5 million simulated periods each (Annex B, randomised manoeuvre statistics, quiet targets, correlated errors and outliers), a T4 each, $14 in all. Its reported track is the arc model fitted to the bearings at the manoeuvres the model declares.

The plan, the training mix, the criteria and the code were bound by digest before the first training run and before the validation and test seeds existed. The scorer refused to score a learned track until the controls' own validation was on record.

The registered outcome (test seed 341, 2,860 periods)​

Declared control ÷ learned track, paired per period, three seeds (above 1: the learned track is better):

SplitRatioVerdict
Shifted prior0.82, 0.80, 0.82not shown
Shifted prior 20.87, 0.87, 0.94not shown
Correlated errors0.83, 0.83, 0.84not shown
Outliers0.78, 0.77, 0.81not shown
Bias, absent from training0.98, 1.00, 0.97not shown
Annex B0.82, 0.81, 0.82harm
Held course1.06, 1.06, 1.06no harm

Learning is shown on no split and there is harm on Annex B data: the classical controls stand as the time-late system, and the learned track stops. The forecast written before training said this was the most likely outcome.

What the classical controls did​

Against the search they started from, the declared control is 1.68 [1.46, 1.94] better with 2% outliers, 2.44 [2.03, 3.00] with 5%, 1.33 [1.16, 1.53] with correlated errors and 1.70 [1.48, 1.95] on targets that never manoeuvre (false manoeuvres in 8% of periods against 49%). These replicate across the tuning, validation and test seeds. This is the result the panel says is worth carrying.

It has limits the first record understated. Under a slowly varying bias it does nothing (1.00). On clean data its range error is not separated from the search's over three seeds (0.96 to 1.09). It calls a one-manoeuvre target quiet more often, markedly so with correlated errors (0.29 against 0.05). Its correlated-error form knows the simulator's error family. And under a shifted manoeuvre prior it gains nothing (1.03): the control is still 1.7 to 2.1 times a fit told the true history, whichever way that reference is fitted.

What the learned model's loss is made of​

Five reviewers recomputed the outcome and it holds: all 42 ratios reproduce, no verdict is near its boundary, the registration held. Then they took the 20% apart.

The typical period is a tie. The median per-period ratio is 1.00 on every split. Where the model declares the same number of manoeuvres as the control, the two tracks are level (0.95 on Annex B, 1.01 under the shifted prior), because the read-out is then the same classical fit. Where the model declares fewer, in a quarter to a half of periods, its track is about twice as bad. The whole loss is there.

So the registered comparison measured a detector. The model's manoeuvre probability was thresholded at 0.5, a value never tuned, while the control's margin and quiet probability were tuned. That asymmetry was in the registration and was mine. A reviewer tried the obvious repairs on spent tuning data: a lower threshold makes the read-out worse (the fit can no more remove a false manoeuvre than add a missed one), and a broader prior changes nothing. Starting the control's own search from the model's answer equals the control at a third of the search time, and does not beat it.

The model as an estimator (its own output, reported beside and deciding nothing) is 0.71 of the control on Annex B data. Under the shifted prior it is level in range, 1.01, but behind in course and speed (0.79, 0.77), and the level figure is a cancellation: it beats the control where the bearings determine little and is nearly three times worse where they determine much. That is the signature of an estimator that leans on what it learned about targets in general, which this project has now seen three times.

The "mismatch" was the classical side's only. The shifted, correlated and outlier conditions all lie inside the model's training ranges. The model lost in-distribution.

What was not delivered​

  • A working prior-mismatch diagnostic: the one computed is not a Bayes factor and fires on quiet targets, not on a shifted prior.
  • A Huber cost and a whitened fit (editing and an effective sd stand in), and the repair of the evidence at the edges of the prior's support.
  • The export check on the trained models (it ran on a toy), IMM and EKF tracks beside, and the weights' digests in the test record.
  • Unit tests for the runner and the scorer.
  • Two launches of the GPU pilot failed at start-up on a launcher form that had never been run; the ledger under-counts a run whose container is replaced (39 cents against the owner's dashboard).

What this does and does not show​

It shows that a small direct model, trained on the simulator, does not beat an evidence search that knows the motion model, in or out of the conditions it was trained on, and that classical editing and an honest bearing sd remove most of the damage from outliers and correlated errors.

It does not show that learning cannot help the time-late consumer. A learned proposer inside the search, the model's probabilities as a prior, training through the arc model, and a larger budget were not tested. Nor does it show that the shifted-prior gap can be closed by anything: busier targets with smaller turns may simply not be identifiable from bearings, and that is the cheapest next thing to find out.

Across specs 012 to 016 the founding question stands at "not shown, at small budgets, with direct models". Each large gain so far has gone to a classical element.

Records​

experiments/20261113-tl4-tuning/, -tl4-decision/ (two addenda), -tl4-val/, experiments/20261114-tlm-runs/, and the test record experiments/20261114-tl4/ (review.md). Seeds 338 to 341 are used; the next fresh seed is 342. GPU spending in November stands at about $41 of the owner's $50.

item.content:encoded:
The owner has chosen to build the classical controls the last panel asked for and, at the same time, to train a learned whole-period model on GPU under a plan registered before any result. The model is scored only once the controls exist. Spec: specs/016-time-late-learned/.

Where we are​

Spec 015 repaired the evidence, the edge rule and the reference and decided the same quantities again on fresh seeds. The registered rule again gave no GPU budget for identification on Annex B data, and the panel showed that 400 periods cannot decide a 10% line there. Carried: the repaired evidence-scored search as the standing time-late system, and C″ read as a track as the control beneath it. Open: against a reference told the true history the search is 1.7 times worse under a shifted manoeuvre prior, 1.4 under correlated bearing errors and 1.5 with outliers, and it invents a manoeuvre on half of quiet targets. No classical remedy has been tried for any of these, and neither study said anything about hedging.

Where this task moves to​

SRD §1 (the time-late consumer), §3 (the reported estimate comes from a declared read-out) and §5 (a new row, proposed; the owner merges). Two tracks:

  1. Controls, CPU, nothing trained. A hedged track (the probability-weighted mean of the search's candidates) and a declaration margin; a robust likelihood and a correlated-error likelihood in the search; a broadened manoeuvre prior with a mismatch diagnostic. Settings on tuning seed 338.
  2. A learned model, GPU. A sequence model reads the whole period and gives the whole track, trained on the fly on a declared mix (Annex B, shifted and broadened statistics, quiet targets, correlated errors, outliers), three seeds, within the unspent part of the $50 budget.
  3. Registration first. The model's plan, training mix, comparison and criteria are bound by digest in a decision record before the first training job. No criterion is registered that the sample size cannot decide.
  4. Controls' validation (seed 340) is recorded; only then may the model be scored.
  5. One test scoring (seed 341): the model against the best classical control on each split, with the hedged track beside it; a win is named for the control that explains it, and only what remains is called learning.
  6. Panel, write-up, slides.

Risks: the budget buys too little training to be a fair test; the controls close the gaps and leave nothing to compare (still a result); a sixth error in the evidence; the model wins by knowing the simulator's training mix, which is why one condition is held out of it. We stop before the test seed if the controls' validation run is unsound, and no GPU job runs beyond the ledger's cap.

How progress will be shown​

  • Each control against the plain search on its own split, at two severities (validation 340, test 341): paired ratio and share of the gap to the reference closed.
  • Held course: false manoeuvres against one-manoeuvre targets called quiet, as a curve over the declaration margin (tuning 338).
  • The learned model's training curves for three seeds and the ledger in dollars.
  • One table per split: plain search, best control, hedged track, learned model, reference.
  • Track plots of a few periods where the systems differ, if the tracks are stored this time.
  • All from committed experiment folders by a script named in the slides post.

Update, 2026-11-14. The study ran. The classical controls remove most of the damage from outliers and correlated bearing errors and from quiet targets; the learned model's reported track beats the control on no split, so by the registered rule the controls stand. The panel approved and showed the loss is the model's untuned manoeuvre detector, not a typical period. See the write-up and the slides.
